entries.title: The FAA halts departures nationwide; planes wait at Logan
entries.caption: On Friday afternoon the FAA stopped departing flights at airports across the U.S., citing communications and radar problems at air traffic control centers. At Boston Logan, departures were held while some transatlantic flights left case by case. Homeland Security said there was no sign of an attack; the cause is under investigation. The stop was lifted that evening, after a little over four hours.

stories.name: FAA halts departures nationwide
facts: On Friday afternoon, Nov. 13, the FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop of departing flights at U.S. airports, citing 'extraordinary circumstances' and safety, after communications and radar problems affecting air traffic control centers.
Flights already in the air continued; hundreds were diverted or returned to their departure airports, and thousands of departures were held or cancelled.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication of an attack and called it a telecommunications outage; the cause remained under investigation.
The FAA lifted the ground stop Friday evening, a little over four hours later, allowing departures to resume.
At Boston Logan, departures were held on the ground while some transatlantic flights were allowed to leave case by case; FlightAware showed 92 delays and 17 cancellations just after 5:30 p.m.

entries.title: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia's chief executive
entries.caption: Nvidia announced Thursday that co-founder Jensen Huang had stepped down as CEO and from its board, effective immediately, after 33 years leading the chipmaker; CFO Colette Kress became interim CEO. Shares fell as much as 14% before closing down about 4%. The exit followed days of reports about Huang's personal relationships and related national security questions, which the company says it is investigating.

stories.name: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO
facts: On Thursday, Nov. 12, Nvidia announced that co-founder Jensen Huang had stepped down as CEO and from its board, effective immediately, after 33 years leading the chipmaker.
CFO Colette Kress was named interim CEO while keeping her finance role; Harvey C. Jones became the board's first-ever chair. The board will consider internal and external candidates.
The exit followed days of reports about Huang's personal relationships and related national security questions, which Nvidia said it was investigating; Huang made no public statement reported.
Nvidia shares fell as much as 14% early Thursday, then recovered to close down about 4.3%.

entries.title: Colom wins Mississippi's Senate race after a long count
entries.caption: Democrat Scott Colom, a district attorney, was projected Wednesday to have defeated Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith after officials spent days processing absentee and affidavit ballots; Hyde-Smith conceded by video that evening. Colom will be Mississippi's first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction, and the result flips a deep-red seat. The magnolia, Mississippi's state flower, is symbolic.

stories.name: Democrat Scott Colom defeats Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi
facts: On Wednesday, Nov. 11, the AP, NBC News and CBS News projected that Democrat Scott Colom, a 43-year-old district attorney, had defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi's U.S. Senate race.
The race was extremely close after Election Day; local officials spent several days processing absentee and affidavit ballots before the call, and Colom's narrow lead grew as counting went on.
Hyde-Smith conceded Wednesday evening in a video message, congratulating Colom. He will be Mississippi's first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction.

entries.title: House Republicans elect Jim Jordan as their leader
entries.caption: Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio gives brief remarks after House Republicans chose him to lead them in the next Congress, beating Majority Leader Steve Scalise 106 to 73 in a secret ballot on Nov. 10. The party moves into the minority after its midterm losses, with Speaker Mike Johnson stepping down from leadership. The swirl of blank ballots around the Capitol dome is symbolic.

stories.name: House Republicans elect Jim Jordan as their leader for the next Congress
facts: On Tuesday, Nov. 10, House Republicans who will serve in the next Congress chose Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio, the Judiciary Committee chairman, to lead them in the minority, beating Majority Leader Steve Scalise of Louisiana 106 to 73 in a secret ballot at the Capitol.

The vote follows the party's midterm losses; Speaker Mike Johnson is stepping down from leadership. Democrats hold their leadership elections next week, with Hakeem Jeffries expected to become speaker.
After the vote Jordan gave brief remarks, saying House Republicans will fight for American families over the next two years.

entries.title: Massie files impeachment articles against Hegseth
entries.caption: Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) introduced eight articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on the House floor on Nov. 9, centred on the Iran war being waged without congressional authorization. Because the resolution is privileged, House leaders must table, refer or vote on it within two legislative days. Hegseth called the effort a sham.

stories.name: Rep. Thomas Massie files articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth
facts: On Monday, Nov. 9, Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) introduced and read on the House floor a resolution with eight articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, then discussed it at a news conference on Capitol Hill.
The articles focus mainly on waging the war with Iran without congressional authorization, and also cite the Caribbean boat strikes and the Pentagon's scrutiny of Sen. Mark Kelly.

Impeachment resolutions are privileged, so House leaders must act (table, refer or vote) within two legislative days. Speaker Mike Johnson opposed it; Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries supports it; Hegseth called the effort a sham and scheduled a Tuesday news conference.

entries.title: Larson clinches a third NASCAR Cup title
entries.caption: Kyle Larson clinched his third NASCAR Cup Series championship at Homestead-Miami Speedway on Nov. 8, locking it up on points at the end of Stage 1, under caution, while crew chief Cliff Daniels and owner Rick Hendrick celebrated atop the pit box. Larson finished 12th; Ryan Blaney won the race. Larson is the first back-to-back champion since Jimmie Johnson.

stories.name: Kyle Larson clinches his third NASCAR Cup Series championship
facts: At the season finale at Homestead-Miami Speedway on Sunday, Nov. 8, Kyle Larson (Hendrick Motorsports, No. 5 Chevrolet) clinched the 2026 Cup Series title by finishing fourth in Stage 1, which ended under caution after Chase Briscoe's engine failure.
Larson finished the race 12th and won the title by 49 points over Christopher Bell; Ryan Blaney won the race, passing Tyler Reddick on the last lap.
It is Larson's third Cup title and second in a row, making him the first back-to-back champion since Jimmie Johnson. Crew chief Cliff Daniels and team owner Rick Hendrick celebrated atop the pit box.

entries.title: Trump offers UFC chief Dana White the press secretary job
entries.caption: President Trump said on Truth Social on Nov. 7 that he had offered UFC CEO Dana White the job of White House press secretary. At a news conference in London, White said he was flying to Washington for a Monday meeting but did not say whether he would accept. The post has been vacant since mid-October; the empty podium marks the unanswered offer.

stories.name: Trump offers UFC chief Dana White the White House press secretary job
facts: On Saturday, Nov. 7, President Trump said in a Truth Social post that he had offered UFC CEO Dana White the job of White House press secretary; some outlets noted it was unclear how serious the offer was.
Speaking at a boxing event news conference in London on Saturday, White said he was flying to Washington and had a meeting on Monday; he did not say whether he would accept.
The press secretary post has been vacant since mid-October, after Karoline Leavitt left in August and her successor Katie Zacharia departed after five days.

entries.title: Stephen Miller replaces Susie Wiles as chief of staff
entries.caption: On Nov. 6, President Trump announced on Truth Social that deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller will replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff, starting Monday. Wiles, the first woman in the job, said Friday was her last day. The first major shake-up after Republicans lost Congress in the midterms elevates the architect of the administration's immigration crackdown.

stories.name: Stephen Miller replaces Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff
facts: On Friday, Nov. 6, President Trump announced on Truth Social that deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller will replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff; his post said Miller starts Monday.
Wiles, the first woman to hold the post, posted that Friday was her last day, calling the job the honor of a lifetime; Trump said she will move to his political operation.
The change came days after Republicans lost control of Congress in the midterm elections; Miller is known as the architect of the administration's immigration enforcement and deportation policies.

entries.title: Newsom commutes California's 548 death sentences
entries.caption: California Gov. Gavin Newsom reduced the sentences of all 548 people on the state's death row to life without parole, announcing it in an open letter to Californians. Some cases still need California Supreme Court review, and victims' groups criticized the blanket move. The state has not executed anyone since 2006 and has been under Newsom's moratorium since 2019.

stories.name: Newsom commutes California's death sentences
facts: On Thursday, Nov. 5, California Gov. Gavin Newsom reduced the sentences of all 548 people on the state's death row to life in prison without the possibility of parole.
He announced it in an open letter to Californians, writing that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values.

Some cases require review by the California Supreme Court (people with two prior felony convictions), and the move could face legal challenges; crime victims' groups criticized it as a blanket decision.
Newsom imposed a moratorium on executions in 2019; California has not executed anyone since 2006.

entries.title: Democrats take the House and Senate
entries.caption: The day after the midterms, CBS News projected that Democrats had won majorities in both the House and the Senate. Speaker Mike Johnson said he would not stay on as Republican leader, and Hakeem Jeffries announced his bid for speaker. The new Congress takes over in January, ending unified Republican control in Washington for President Trump's final two years.

stories.name: Democrats win control of the House and Senate
facts: On Nov. 4, the day after the 2026 midterm elections, CBS News projected that Democrats had won majorities in both the House and the Senate; NBC News also reported Democrats taking both chambers.
Republican Sen. Ted Cruz said on his podcast, "We've lost the House, we've lost the Senate."
House Speaker Mike Johnson told his staff Wednesday morning he will not stay on as Republican leader in the new Congress; Steve Scalise and Jim Jordan announced bids for minority leader.

Hakeem Jeffries announced his candidacy for speaker in a letter to House Democrats; Democratic leaders laid out priorities including lowering costs, restoring ACA subsidies, reversing Medicaid cuts, undoing tariffs and ending the Iran war.
The new Congress begins in January; Mississippi's Senate race was still too close to call that evening.

entries.title: Pappas wins New Hampshire's Senate seat
entries.caption: On midterm Election Day, Democrat Chris Pappas won New Hampshire's open US Senate seat, defeating former Sen. John E. Sununu, who conceded in Manchester; the AP called the race at 8:22 p.m. Pappas becomes the first openly gay man elected to the Senate. The seat stays Democratic; control of Congress was still undecided that night.

stories.name: Pappas wins New Hampshire Senate seat on midterm Election Day
facts: On Nov. 3, Election Day in the 2026 midterms, Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas defeated former Republican Sen. John E. Sununu for New Hampshire's open US Senate seat, left open by retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen.
The Associated Press called the race at 8:22 p.m. Eastern; CBS News and NBC News also projected Pappas the winner.
Sununu conceded in a speech to supporters in Manchester, saying he had called Pappas to congratulate him; Democratic partygoers cheered as word of the concession spread.
Pappas becomes the first openly gay man elected to the US Senate. The win keeps the seat in Democratic hands; control of the Senate and House was still undecided that night.

entries.title: Supreme Court rejects bid to set aside 20,000 California ballots
entries.caption: On Nov. 2, the eve of Election Day, the Supreme Court rejected the Trump administration's emergency request that California set aside up to about 20,000 mail ballots it says came from noncitizens. The brief order gave no reasons; no justice publicly dissented. Lower courts had also refused, and state officials dispute the federal list. The stream of envelopes is symbolic.

stories.name: Supreme Court rejects bid to set aside 20,000 California ballots
facts: On Nov. 2, the day before Election Day, the Supreme Court rejected the Trump administration's emergency request that California set aside up to about 20,000 mail ballots from people the administration says are noncitizens.
The brief order gave no explanation and no justice publicly dissented; the court acted within hours, without first asking California to respond.
Solicitor General D. John Sauer had filed the request that morning after U.S. District Judge David O. Carter denied it and a Ninth Circuit panel upheld him 2-1.

California officials dispute the accuracy of the federal list and warned eligible citizens could be disenfranchised; noncitizen voting is already illegal under state law. Hundreds of thousands of ballots had already been processed.

entries.title: Jet crashes on a Palm Beach County road, killing all nine aboard
entries.caption: A Learjet flying from Austin to the Bahamas crashed nose-first onto Military Trail in Palm Beach County, Florida, on Nov. 1, killing all nine people aboard. It left a burning crater feet from homes; no one on the ground was reported hurt, and about 600 nearby mobile home residents were evacuated. The crew had reported icing and turbulence before a steep dive. The NTSB is investigating; no cause has been determined.

stories.name: Jet crashes on a Palm Beach County road, killing all nine aboard
facts: A Learjet 60 bound from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas crashed around 12:50 p.m. on Nov. 1 near a residential area of Palm Beach County, Florida, coming down nose-first on Military Trail and leaving a burning crater in the road.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said all nine people aboard were killed; their identities had not been released. Gov. Ron DeSantis said there were no immediate reports of anyone hurt on the ground.
Witnesses told AP the jet landed feet from homes and close to passing vehicles. Thick black smoke covered the site; the road was closed in both directions.
Authorities evacuated about 600 residents of a nearby mobile home community. Rain was falling and a flood watch was in effect.
The NTSB is investigating with FAA support. Air traffic audio shows the crew reported icing and turbulence and asked to climb before a steep dive and a mayday; no cause has been determined.

entries.title: Virginia and D.C. sue to block Trump's planned arch
entries.caption: Virginia and the District of Columbia sued in federal court on Oct. 31 to stop the planned 250-foot arch at Memorial Circle, beside the bridge to Arlington National Cemetery, the third lawsuit against it. They warn of years of traffic, runoff and emergency-response disruption. The administration says work could start next week. The unbuilt arch appears here only as a blueprint outline.

stories.name: Virginia and D.C. sue to block Trump's planned arch
facts: On Oct. 31, Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones and D.C. Attorney General Brian Schwalb sued in federal court to stop the planned arch, seeking a temporary restraining order. It is the third lawsuit against the project.

The arch would rise about 250 feet on a grassy site at Memorial Circle, off the bridge between Washington and Arlington National Cemetery. Plans describe a winged bronze Lady Liberty holding a torch with an eternal flame on top.

The states say about three years of construction would snarl traffic between D.C. and Virginia, add Potomac runoff and hinder emergency services; they also cite height, commemorative-works, environmental and historic-preservation laws.

The administration says construction could begin as early as next week, after a National Capital Planning Commission vote. The White House calls the arch a gateway to Arlington National Cemetery. Judge Tanya Chutkan has not yet ruled in the first lawsuit.

entries.title: Pope Leo XIV votes by mail in the US midterms
entries.caption: The Vatican confirmed that Pope Leo XIV, born in Chicago, cast a mail-in ballot in Illinois ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections. He is the first pope to vote in a U.S. general election. Local officials said he requested the ballot on Oct. 3; how he voted is not known.

stories.name: Pope Leo XIV votes by mail in the US midterms
facts: The Holy See press office confirmed on Oct. 30 that Pope Leo XIV, born Robert Prevost in Chicago, cast a mail-in ballot in Illinois ahead of the Nov. 3 U.S. midterm elections. He is the first pope to vote in a U.S. general election.
The Chicago Sun-Times first reported the vote, citing the Will County clerk's office, which said he requested the mail-in ballot on Oct. 3. He is registered at an address in New Lenox, Illinois.
The Vatican said he has voted whenever he was eligible, including while living in Peru. Who he voted for is not known.

entries.title: Probes into Alaska's two-Sullivan Senate ballot
entries.caption: Alaska's Senate ballot lists two Sullivans: Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan and Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. After a New York Times report that a Democratic operative helped recruit the second, Gov. Mike Dunleavy ordered a state investigation, and CBS News reported new Justice Department subpoenas. No one has been charged; Mary Peltola's campaign denies involvement. The election is Nov. 3.

stories.name: Probes into Alaska's two-Dan-Sullivan Senate ballot
facts: Alaska's Senate ballot lists two men named Sullivan: Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan and Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a retired rural teacher listed with no party. A state elections official tried to bar him in June; courts restored him.

On Oct. 28, after a New York Times report that a Democratic operative working with Mary Peltola's campaign helped encourage Daniel J. Sullivan to run, Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy ordered the Department of Public Safety to investigate.
On Oct. 29, CBS News reported, citing sources, that the Justice Department issued a new wave of subpoenas to Democratic officials believed tied to the recruitment effort. No one has been charged.

Peltola's campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee deny involvement; Daniel J. Sullivan has said he genuinely wants to run. Trump repeated calls for Peltola to be prosecuted on Oct. 29.

entries.title: Dolores Huerta, farmworker organizer, dies at 96
entries.caption: Dolores Huerta, who co-founded the farmworkers' union that became the United Farm Workers with Cesar Chavez in 1962, died Oct. 28 at her home in Bakersfield, California, at 96; her family said the cause was cancer. Shown in tribute: the 1960s Delano grape strike picket line she marched on. She coined the rallying cry "Sí se puede" and received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2012.

stories.name: Labor and civil rights leader Dolores Huerta dies at 96
facts: Dolores Huerta died on Wednesday, Oct. 28, at 96, at her home in Bakersfield, California, surrounded by family; a family spokesperson said the cause was cancer.
In 1962 she and Cesar Chavez founded the National Farm Workers Association, which became the United Farm Workers; she served as its vice president until 1999.

She joined Filipino grape pickers on the picket line in the five-year Delano grape strike and led national grape and lettuce boycotts in the early 1970s, which helped win California's 1975 law recognizing farmworkers' right to bargain collectively.
She coined the rallying cry 'Sí se puede'. President Obama awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2012.

entries.title: Grand jury declines to indict Cassidy Hutchinson
entries.caption: A federal grand jury in Washington declined the Justice Department's request to indict Cassidy Hutchinson, the former White House aide who was the House Jan. 6 committee's star witness in 2022, according to people familiar with the case. Republican lawmakers had accused her of lying under oath; the charges sought were not made public. It is another setback in the department's cases against Trump critics.

stories.name: Grand jury declines to indict Cassidy Hutchinson
facts: A federal grand jury in Washington declined the Justice Department's request to indict Cassidy Hutchinson, a former aide to Trump chief of staff Mark Meadows, according to people familiar with the proceedings.
A Justice Department lawyer told a magistrate judge at an unrelated hearing on Tuesday that a grand jury had not concurred on a proposed indictment; sources said the defendant was Hutchinson.
Hutchinson was a star witness at the House Jan. 6 committee's 2022 hearings; Republican lawmakers had accused her of lying under oath. The exact charges sought were not made public.
Neither Hutchinson nor the Justice Department commented publicly in the first reports.

entries.title: Comey charged a third time
entries.caption: Former FBI Director James Comey, charged with transmitting national defense information in court papers unsealed Monday, says in a video statement that he is innocent. Prosecutors tie the case to a 2016 New York Times story; his lawyers say the charges, filed without a grand jury indictment, are time-barred. It is the Justice Department's third attempt to prosecute him in about a year.

stories.name: James Comey charged a third time
facts: Federal prosecutors charged former FBI Director James Comey with transmitting national defense information and conspiring to do so, in court papers unsealed Monday.
The case concerns an October 2016 New York Times story about a secret court order for Yahoo to scan emails; prosecutors say Comey had staff talk to the reporter.
The charges were filed as a criminal information, not a grand jury indictment; Comey's lawyers say they are time-barred. It is the third attempt to prosecute him in about a year.
Comey said in a video statement that he is innocent.

entries.title: Machado returns to Venezuela
entries.caption: María Corina Machado, Venezuela's opposition leader and 2025 Nobel Peace Prize laureate, is embraced by supporters at a church in Lara state after about ten months abroad. "I am here. With you," she wrote on announcing her return. Venezuela has been run by an acting president with US backing since the US military removed Nicolás Maduro in January; no election has been scheduled.

stories.name: María Corina Machado returns to Venezuela
facts: Opposition leader and 2025 Nobel Peace Prize laureate María Corina Machado returned to Venezuela after about 10 months abroad, announcing: "I am here. With you."
She was seen at a church in Lara state, where dozens of supporters greeted and hugged her, some recording on raised phones (AP).
Venezuela has been run by acting president Delcy Rodríguez, with US backing, since the US military removed Nicolás Maduro in January 2026; no election has been scheduled.

entries.title: Trump votes early as Obama returns to the trail
entries.caption: President Trump, wearing an "I Voted" sticker, talks to reporters after casting his midterm ballot early in West Palm Beach, Florida, with Melania Trump beside him. That evening, former President Barack Obama, back on the campaign trail after a first stop in Cleveland, rallied Democrats in a Detroit high-school gym, calling Trump's second term "two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption."

stories.name: Trump votes early as Obama returns to the campaign trail
facts: On Saturday, October 24, President Trump cast his midterm ballot early at the Palm Beach County Supervisor of Elections office in West Palm Beach, Florida, arriving with first lady Melania Trump.
Wearing an "I Voted" sticker, he told reporters he had voted the Republican line: "Very much so."

The same day, former President Barack Obama held his first midterm rally in Cleveland with Democratic nominees Sherrod Brown and Amy Acton, then spoke at an evening rally in a Detroit high-school gym.
Obama called Trump's second term "two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption."
